audit.recode_to: No class change: fixed-dominant penultimate (non-strict) matches the OPD's 'generally on the penultimate syllable'. Replace the Wikipedia quote/cite with OPD p.4 sec. 1.1.4 and drop 'always'.
audit.deciding_source_kind: database or survey citing another work
audit.reasoning: The record's classification (fixed-dominant, penult, not in the strict set) rests on a Wikipedia sentence with no copies we hold. The primary it cites, the SIL-PNG Organised Phonology Data (Landweer 2000, rev. Schulz 2012, 12 pp., archive 64101), was located through the archived SIL listing and downloaded; p.4 sec. 1.1.4 reads 'Stress is generally on the penultimate syllable and does not need to be indicated orthographically.' The ~60 stress-marked transcriptions are penultimate with alternating secondary stress, one final-stress token on a CVC-final word ([mɑˈtɑm]) and final diphthongs counted as one syllable -- consistent with a dominant (not exceptionless) penult rule, so the classification stands but the quotation overstates ('always'). Glottolog 5.1 has zero grammar/phonology entries for Anuki and the SIL listing holds only this OPD plus sociolinguistic and literacy items, so the OPD is the best available d

sources.quote: "Stress is generally on the penultimate syllable and does not need to be indicated orthographically. Tone is not phonemic." Stress-marked transcriptions are overwhelmingly penultimate ([biˈnɑmɑ], [poˈpoku], [midiˈmidi], [epɑˈmɑnɑ]); secondary stresses alternate leftward ([wɑˌsikuˈwɑjɑ], [iviˌnuwɑˌnuwɑˈnedɑ]); one final-stress token on a closed final syllable ([mɑˈtɑm] 'tomorrow') and final diphthongs treated as monosyllabic ([ˈkɑpoᵉ], [kiˈɾɑkɨⁱ], [ˈbubɑᵘ]).
